transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-10 16:00 UTC; Duration ~38 min; Attendees listed above.

Summary: quick phone screen for Solutions Architect role. Focus areas: inference serving experience, troubleshooting at scale, customer-facing consulting examples, security/compliance exposure, culture fit. Candidate currently at Nimbus Health working on ML infra for clinical NLP.

Topics: intro, background, technical depth, oncall/examples, expectations, next steps.

00:00 Samir: hey Aaron thanks for making time, quick intro from our side, i'm Samir, AE, and Diane who manages the infra hiring, Tom from recruiting on the line. can you do a 30-40 minute quick screen?
00:12 Aaron: yeah absolutely, thanks for the invite, excited to chat. i'm Aaron, i've been at Nimbus for three years building inference pipelines for clinical models, mostly private deployments and hybrid clouds.
00:24 Diane: great, high level, what's the scale you were running? latency/throughput numbers?
00:30 Aaron: so typically inference is mixed, we run a hosted edge for smaller endpoints and dedicated gpu pools for batch. P95 latencies around 80-180ms for short text tasks on our transformer models at 512 tokens, throughput for dedicated pools around 500-800 tokens/sec per GPU depending on batching, we use cuBLAS/aten kernels, and we rolled some custom fused kernels in one place, the performance varied.
01:05 Tom: (background noise) okay.
01:08 Diane: did you own the serving runtime or were you integrating third-party endpoints?
01:12 Aaron: mostly owned, we started with huggingface transformers + torchserve, then migrated components to a custom async runtime to reduce context switching, implemented a prefix caching layer (we called it K V cash, spelled K-V-cash in notes — we actually mean KV cache) which saved 20-30% of token compute for chat flows. There were some mis-synced cache invalidation bugs once with rolling deploys, learned to tie cache key versions to model version.
01:44 Samir: nice. any experience with quantization and the tradeoffs?
01:47 Aaron: yeah, we've applied 4/8-bit quant profiles, observed small quality delta on clinical NER but big throughput gains. our rule was run evals against known prompt suites and set guardrails: if exact F1 drop > 1.5% we didn't quantize. The tooling was rough — we used bitsandbytes and custom per-layer calibration. I do know quan-tee-zation pipelines get messy with certain ops.
02:19 Diane: good. tell us about a tough production incident you handled end-to-end?
02:23 Aaron: one incident — overnight batch workloads saturated GPUs due to a bad feature change that increased sequence lengths. autoscaler didn't react fast enough because it was configured on pod cpu/mem rather than queue depth and token rate. We had to add a token-rate metric to the HPA, add backpressure at the ingress, and implement a rapid fallback routing to smaller model variants which kept latency stable. I coordinated incident comms, wrote postmortem, and led the rollout of improved autoscaling.
03:10 Samir: how much of the work was infra vs product stakeholder management?
03:14 Aaron: probably 60/40 infra, because we were small, but I was customer-facing — ran onboarding with their security teams, handled SSO/SAML handshake, KMS integration for keys, and documented audit log retention for SOC2 requests.
03:30 Diane: any private deployment or VPC/on-prem experience?
03:33 Aaron: yes, we deployed to customer-managed VPCs and had an on-prem option for a couple hospitals. we integrate with their HSM for key wrapping, and often had to support air-gapped installs where we shipped docker bundles and a migration guide.
03:50 Tom: (soft) what's your oncall cadence today?
03:52 Aaron: 1:6 rotation, pager flips maybe 2-3 incidents a month, most are perf regressions or OOMs after a model update. I also do runbooks and blameless postmortems.
04:08 Diane: How comfortable are you with kernel-level GPU debugging or profiling? can you work with low-level perf tools?
04:13 Aaron: comfortable — I've used nvprof, nsight, triton profiler, and sometimes instrumented at CUDA async streams. In one project we worked with custom fused operators and had to tune occupancy and memory alignment for better cache lines. I'm not a CUDA kernel author day-to-day but I can read and reason about them and work with a lower-level engineer.
04:39 Samir: Customer-facing consulting — how do you handle expectations around latency vs cost, for example dedicated vs hosted?
04:46 Aaron: I frame it as SLOs + unit economics; if the customer needs p50<50ms we recommend pinned low-batch dedicated instances and aggressive caching, accept higher cost; for p95-sensitive applications we talk about model distillation or smaller context windows, and show cost modeling spreadsheets. We run A/B with canary routing to measure customer impact.
05:12 Diane: any experience with rollout strategies like canary, A/B, automatic fallback?
05:16 Aaron: yes, canary percentages, traffic shadowing, and automatic fallback to cheaper variants if latency or error-rate thresholds breach. Also mix of model-versioned cache invalidation so we don't serve stale cache to canaries.
05:30 Samir: do you have experience writing customer-facing docs or onboarding guides?
05:34 Aaron: lots. I maintain a playbook for private deploys, security checklist, and run a templated onboarding deck.
05:42 Diane: culture fit — how do you work with product and sales when there are conflicts about shipping features vs reliability?
05:48 Aaron: I negotiate by proposing safety nets: feature flags, observability hooks, and SLO-based gating. I prefer measurable compromises: if a feature ships with a 10% increased resource cost, we set a budget and test it with limited rollouts.
06:07 Tom: recruiter question — compensation expectations?
06:10 Aaron: i'm targeting 180-230k base depending on role and equity, flexible on structure.
06:19 Samir: quick technical: how do you approach KV cache invalidation on model upgrades with rolling deploys?
06:24 Aaron: tie cache keys to model git sha + tokenizer version + config fingerprint; apply a grace period where old cache still served for zero-downtime, or better we version the cache namespace and migrate entries lazily. But be careful with memory blowup — have an eviction policy and monitor miss storms after deploy.
06:52 Diane: do you have hands-on with routing policies and smart routing for cost vs latency?
06:56 Aaron: yes, implemented priority queues and cost-aware routing — cheaper region or smaller model on background tasks, pinned region for high-sensitivity data. Used a policy engine to route by tenant tier.
07:10 Samir: any familiarity with Redwood-like product patterns: hosted API, dedicated, private, observability.
07:17 Aaron: yes, familiar conceptually; I've used hosted offerings and built private variants. Observability-wise we've used per-route histograms, token-level cost accounting and alerting, and surfaced regressions with CI against prompt suites.
07:35 Diane: do you have any concerns about switching to a small startup model?
07:39 Aaron: i like high impact and cross-functional work but want clarity on career ladder and mentorship.
07:47 Samir: great. behavioral question — lead a customer who wants unencrypted logs for debugging but legal says no. how do you approach?
07:55 Aaron: negotiate a proxy: ephemeral scrubbed logs, secure enclaves, structured logs with PII redaction, or a runbook where logs are shared only via a secure channel under NDA and data use agreement. emphasize audit logging.
08:15 Diane: what would you want to see from us if we moved forward?
08:18 Aaron: a clear interview loop, a technical deep dive with infra team, and a chance to see the product and org chart. also the take-home exercise to show design tradeoffs.
08:28 Tom: we'll send the exercise, couple available dates for technical deep-dive.
08:33 Samir: final quick wrap, any other big projects to flag?
08:36 Aaron: we've been migrating to a regionally-aware edge strategy and working on multitenant isolation at the inference level, which was fun.
08:42 Diane: thanks Aaron, we'll follow up with next steps.

Notes on transcription: small mis-hears (K V cash vs KV cache, quan-tee-zation phrasing). Natural speech fillers present.

End meeting.
